title: High potassium in CKD on spironolactone — recognising and responding to a time-critical presentation

blocks.text: High potassium in CKD on spironolactone — recognising and responding to a time-critical presentation
AMaC MRCP PACES23 · R5-204 · Station 2, acute consultation · Skills A–G (focus C, E, F, G) · 20 minutes · Prepared 14 October 2026 · Educational simulation; not an official PACES mark scheme.

A 70-year-old with chronic kidney disease taking spironolactone has a laboratory potassium of 6.8 mmol/L and feels weak. Speak to the patient (and accompanying person if applicable), identify immediate risks and explain your management plan. The examiner may provide results on request.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: HOOK — Severe hyperkalaemia potentially driven by CKD and potassium-retaining drugs; a normal ECG cannot safely exclude dangerous hyperkalaemia.

TRAP — Calcium stabilises the myocardium but does not lower potassium. Avoid undersized calcium dosing: UKKA specifies 30 mL of 10% calcium gluconate IV (or 10 mL of 10% calcium chloride via a large or central vein), repeated if ECG changes persist; follow local medicines guidance, including post-insulin hypoglycaemia surveillance. Withhold/review spironolactone and other contributors.

If ECG changes or peri-arrest, give IV calcium per UKKA (30 mL of 10% calcium gluconate IV (or 10 mL of 10% calcium chloride via a large or central vein), repeated if ECG changes persist) to protect myocardium; use insulin–glucose to shift potassium, consider nebulised salbutamol and appropriate potassium removal with binder/dialysis pathway. Repeat potassium and monitor capillary glucose following insulin.

blocks.text: Patient: “I feel weak, but my heart feels normal. Could the test be wrong?” If asked, you have CKD and take spironolactone; mention any potassium supplements only if questioned. You are anxious about going to hospital. If reassured despite potassium 6.8, ask, “Could this affect my heart?”

History and examination information available when requested: Check for haemolysis or sample error without delaying care; symptoms, pulse, blood pressure, ECG, renal function, urine output, medication list and dietary/potassium supplement intake.

Q1 EXAMINER: “Is potassium 6.8 mmol/L urgent if the ECG looks normal?” MODEL: Yes. Severe hyperkalaemia can cause abrupt life-threatening arrhythmia; do not use a normal ECG to dismiss the laboratory result.
Q2 EXAMINER: “What should be done first?” MODEL: ABCDE, cardiac monitoring, 12-lead ECG, urgent senior help and a timely repeat sample if appropriate without delaying therapy.

Q3 EXAMINER: “When is IV calcium indicated and what does it do?” MODEL: For ECG changes or peri-arrest in severe hyperkalaemia, IV calcium stabilises cardiac excitability but does not lower serum potassium; give the UKKA dose (30 mL of 10% calcium gluconate IV (or 10 mL of 10% calcium chloride via a large or central vein), repeated if ECG changes persist).

Q4 EXAMINER: “How is potassium shifted and removed?” MODEL: Insulin–glucose therapy, adjunct nebulised salbutamol where appropriate, measures to remove potassium, and renal review for refractory hyperkalaemia.

Q5 EXAMINER: “What follow-up and prevention are required?” MODEL: Repeat potassium and ECG, post-insulin glucose monitoring, review spironolactone and other potassium-raising drugs and evaluate AKI/CKD.
Curveball: Patient becomes hypotensive or less responsive. Candidate must stop routine questioning, call for help, reassess ABCDE, monitor and treat reversible causes.

FAIL — CANDIDATE: “You have no chest pain, so the high potassium can wait.” PATIENT: “Could it hurt my heart?” CANDIDATE: “No monitoring is necessary.” [Unsafe failure of escalation.]

PASS — CANDIDATE: “A potassium of 6.8 is dangerously high even if your heart feels normal. I am arranging immediate ECG and monitoring and involving senior colleagues. We will treat the potassium and review spironolactone.” PATIENT: “Is the treatment risky?” CANDIDATE: “We will monitor potassium and blood glucose closely.”

HIGH-PERFORMANCE — CANDIDATE: “This is severe hyperkalaemia. We need continuous monitoring, ECG, rapid assessment for renal deterioration and urgent potassium-lowering treatment. If ECG changes are present, IV calcium (30 mL of 10% calcium gluconate, repeated if ECG changes persist) protects the heart while insulin–glucose and other measures lower potassium. We will check for rebound and hypoglycaemia, stop contributing drugs and involve renal specialists if refractory.”
R2/R4: Overlooks discriminating presentation: Severe hyperkalaemia potentially driven by CKD and potassium-retaining drugs; a normal ECG cannot safely exclude dangerous hyperkalaemia.

Repeat potassium and monitor capillary glucose following insulin.

THINK: Severe hyperkalaemia. SAY: recognise urgency. DO: immediately assess, monitor, investigate and treat according to UK protocol. TRAP: A normal ECG does not exclude dangerous hyperkalaemia.
